💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.
  • Industry observers note that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point.
  • The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

Industry observers note that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

Recent findings suggest that the identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron indicates the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Sources indicate that saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert upcoming audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz claims the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

DxO Year in Review 2026: Four New Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • According to recent reports, full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

According to recent reports, full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to fresh licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in Latest Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

DxO released fresh versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

Each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

In a recent development, always looking for upcoming ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

If you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

It has been revealed that pureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a upcoming file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

According to recent reports, in the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

According to recent reports, the lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

In this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a new DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

In a recent development, for noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

It has been revealed that if the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

PureRAW fits a photographer who plans to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the tech giant’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Sources indicate that brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide shows each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

Industry observers note that no matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the upcoming Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

Recent findings suggest that these masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

Sources indicate that an automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

According to recent reports, their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

Recent findings suggest that color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

With the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

It has been revealed that the free 10.3 revision, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

Recent findings suggest that point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

Sources indicate that released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

The photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

In a recent development, the standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 enhancement adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

In a recent development, saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

Recent findings suggest that photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

Industry observers note that rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

That filter, Halation, is one of three latest effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

Sources indicate that chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

Sources indicate that glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

Recent findings suggest that the new Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

Sources indicate that eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

Version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The update also brings 18 new presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

It has been revealed that matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

Sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which shows the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

In a recent development, XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

In a recent development, the finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

Remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

Suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that shows in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

He judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

DxO revealed a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

PhotoLab 10 launched without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 revision, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

Industry observers note that that makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

It has been revealed that nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

Industry observers note that dxO’s Black Friday prices cover fresh licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

In a recent development, nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

Sources indicate that viewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

According to recent reports, filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

Iraq’s national museum confirms reopening after major renovations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December.
  • Several vital artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry.
  • Recent findings suggest that the reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the new government under Ali al-Zaidi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several newly introduced galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Several vital artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The newly introduced Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

Recent findings suggest that the reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the new government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are plans afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an key moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

In a recent development, A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while latest ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has declared that a new museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Al-Dakhili has also declared that the openings of three fresh museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement claims.

#80249. Industry News: The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño

Industry News: The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan.
  • At the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots.
  • Recent findings suggest that irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan. On this island, which is well known as one of Earth’s vital lungs, a vigorous struggle is at the moment taking place on the peatland frontlines, with a group of local mothers at its heart who are defending their community.

At the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots. After waving goodbye to her mother from the simple terrace, she gets ready for her daily shift as a volunteer firefighter in Sungai Putri Village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan. Irma is the coordinator of The Power of Mama, a group of all-women firefighters and environmental conservation volunteers.

Recent findings suggest that irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air. The heat is overwhelming, and morning visibility is severely diminished by an extremely thick layer of toxic smog. “The haze is incredibly dense today.”.

When the smoke becomes heavier, Irma’s children are kept inside and cannot go to school. Air pollution brings all local activities to a standstill. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it,” she indicates. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones who feel its effects most.”.

A huge column of noxious smoke is clearly visible from her front door. “It’s been two kilometers from our house,” Irma says in a hurry and at once throws her leg over the motorcycle, riding off towards the blazing site.

The Power of Mama reveals how the team converts local vigilance into first-line fire defense. The volunteers work in shifts and ride their motorbikes through areas prone to fires. Each day, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. during the dry season, they look for hotspots in the plantation lands and along the forest boundaries, record the coordinates, take photographs, and enter the information into a special app for regular reporting.

Their efforts do not cease once the fires have died down. In the rainy season, the group shifts its focus to conducting community outreach, advising local farmers on fire control and encouraging them to use alternative methods to restore soil nitrogen rather than burning. They carry out the rehabilitation of degraded mangroves and teach children about the vital need for sustainable land management. If a fire is detected, they promptly inform Manggala Agni, the specialized brigade operated by the Ministry of Forestry, which is Indonesia’s main frontline defense against forest and land fires.

Sources indicate that irma, who has been patrolling without rest for three days in a row, mentions that it has not rained since June 22. The area is suffering from a serious water crisis. “The small ditches and even the rivers have dried up, which makes it extremely hard for us to put out the fires,” she notes. “Our only option is to gather with the locals at the borders of the plantation or by the edge of the forest to keep a constant watch on the fire’s progress. I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous.”.

In a recent development, the flames and the suffocating smoke are not the only difficulties that these women have to overcome; in rural Kalimantan, the deeply rooted patriarchal norms caused the mothers’ early attempts to be met with ridicule. Irma remembers the way the mothers were made fun of when they first put on their uniforms.

According to recent reports, she remembers that they were made fun of for wearing uniforms and carrying out patrols. “The men of the village would tease us and say things such as: ‘Are women really patrolling? On serious grounds? Why do women have to patrol? Don’t you have any other duties to perform?'”.

Industry observers note that but their reason is entirely personal. Although Indonesia generally has a dry season from July to October, the weather this year has been surprisingly dry. “There used to be a great deal of wildlife in this area,” Irma recalls wistfully. “We used to see wild boars, deer, muntjacs and even sun bears; we had hornbills, but now it seems as if they have disappeared. The fireflies used to light up the night, but now they are seldom seen.”.

It has been revealed that A deep sense of anxiety exists in Indonesia over the possibility of a catastrophic fire season similar to past disasters. The United Nations has issued worldwide warnings about a Super El Niño phenomenon, which can cause extreme weather, including an abnormally short, very dry monsoon season in Indonesia this year and next. This climate threat means the mothers on patrol consider each fire more dangerous.

The latest meteorological data shows a very bad outlook. According to various global agencies, such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), there is a nearly 69 percent chance that the present Super El Niño will become the strongest ever recorded. The extreme strengthening of this climate pattern is expected to break all previous records. As Daniel Swain, a climate scientist from the University of California, recently pointed out, “This is a truly extraordinary event. We are on the verge of breaking or matching existing records, and the intensity is expected to skyrocket.”.

In a recent development, copernicus ECMWF, an established organization whose climate model data is widely used by scientists worldwide, has issued a special report monitoring aerosol and smoke emissions from forest and land fires in Kalimantan. The pattern shows movement from the southeast to the northwest, consistent with the southeast monsoon. The organization has also noted that the likelihood of higher smoke levels in Kalimantan may continue to rise as El Niño strengthens. Mark Parrington, a senior scientist at ECMWF who works for CAMS, said, “For Indonesia, seasonal fire emissions and regional haze are already higher than normal, in line with what has been seen in previous El Niño years, and we will be keeping a close watch on the situation to understand how the fires and their impact on air quality are changing.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Indonesia, the situation means fire. The country has 20.6 million hectares of tropical peatlands—about 10.8 percent of its total land area. Since peatlands are normally water-saturated and therefore resistant to fire, extensive deforestation and land drainage to grow profitable agricultural products such as palm oil have turned the area into a ready source of ignition. Indonesia possesses the most carbon-dense peatlands in the world; when they are dried out, they become highly flammable and thus pose enormous risks to wildlife, human health, and global biodiversity.

Peat fires are well known for their danger. Unlike surface fires, which burn trees and other plant life in visible flames, peat fires burn beneath the surface. They burn slowly deep in the soil for weeks or months and emit large amounts of methane, carbon monoxide, ozone, and ancient carbon stored in the ground. “It is very difficult to put out peatland fires since the fire is below the surface,” indicates Karmele Llano Sanchez, Director of YIARI (Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia). “You can’t see the flames, but the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.”.

Recent findings suggest that over on another patrol route, Suriati, who is thirty-two, and Ratinah, who is fifty-six, proceed along a narrow and dangerous path towards the edge of the forest. “We’ve already looked at five different spots in three hamlets,” claims Suriati. “Normally we cover a distance of up to 30 kilometers each day, and even allowing for a winding route we manage at least 21 kilometers on average.”.

Recent findings suggest that the ground is harsh. Daily patrols are physically demanding because the paths are filled with sand, loose rocks, and fallen trees. “There are numerous obstacles, particularly during the rainy season when it’s slippery and muddy. We often fall off our motorbikes,” Ratinah remarks with a laugh. Suriati agrees by nodding. “Yes, we do fall a lot. I once burned my leg on the exhaust pipe. In the dry season, we have to fight both dust and thick smoke.”.

Industry observers note that besides detecting fires, their greatest difficulty lies in the field of social engineering—that is, getting their neighbors to abandon the traditional slash-and-burn farming method. “The public’s reaction is the challenge we face most,” admits Suriati, a housewife who operates a small grocery stall. “Sometimes they won’t accept it; they feel that we are showing off or being patronizing. They say, ‘What do motherfolk know?’ When we ask them not to burn the land haphazardly, they can be obstinate. With the older people in particular, we cannot simply forbid them; we have to treat them gently.”.

Ratinah adopts a diplomatic method. “In the case of someone who is clearing land for palm oil, we tell them about the effects thereof. We state, ‘We are not stopping you from clearing the land, but could you please control the fire so that it doesn’t spread?’ We make them aware of the hazards that the smoke poses to the health of their children and families.”.

The Power of Mama was established in 2022 by YIARI, an affiliate of International Animal Rescue. Director Karmele Llano Sanchez formed the movement to empower women and mothers as environmental protectors and as a frontline response to the forest fire crisis. The initiative rests on a central truth: women hold a major role in rural society and possess influence that can help change ingrained behaviors, making them the focus of this story.

In a recent development, “Protecting the forest is one of our main objectives, since fire poses a great threat to it,” Sanchez says. At present, the group includes 146 local women in ten villages in Ketapang. YIARI provides them with rigorous training so they can fight fires directly, operate surveillance drones, and conduct essential community outreach.

For many people, the reason for joining was the trauma from previous fires. Ely Marlina joined because of the terrifying situation she faced while looking after her child during the disastrous 2019 fires. “Many children that year developed respiratory illnesses as a result of the land fires,” she says. In 2019, the crisis involved more than 1,000 hotspots in Ketapang alone, and the notorious 2015 fires also spread, causing the worst pollution of the century, which affected neighboring Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

Industry observers note that the situation in 2026 is just as worrying. The Sipongi website of Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry states that by the end of August 2026, the number of hotspots in Kalimantan had reached 8,638, with West Kalimantan accounting for 3,705, and Ketapang alone having 1,749. More than 202,000 hectares of land had already been burned between January and July 2026, the smoke from the fires spreading across the border into Sarawak, Malaysia, and leading to the closure of almost 600 schools.

Sources indicate that at night in Sungai Awan Kiri Village, the fighting does not stop. Upon receiving a report of a fire near the main road, the team hurries to the spot. “The distance was quite a way away, more than three kilometers from my house, and we got there by motorbike,” says 46-year-old Ely Marlina. “When we jumped into the vehicle while donning our full Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), we discovered that the area on fire was peatland. The ground was very dangerous. My leg even slipped and sank half a meter into the peat.”.

When they arrive, Ely Marlina rapidly gets on a tanker truck and loads water pumps, hoses, and portable tanks onto it. The women then work in perfect coordination as they drag the heavy equipment towards the flames.

The fact that the flames are near the village means action must be taken at once. “There were already some of the residents’ houses about 100 meters away, and the distance to the densely populated residential area was only about 200 or 300 meters,” Ely points out. “We began putting out the fire after the Isha evening prayer, and it wasn’t until 11 p.m. that we were able to bring it under control. The operation took about 4 to 5 hours.”.

Industry observers note that this tense night operation has now become a regular part of their daily routine. “Either we like it or not, since we are volunteers, we have to stay on guard continuously during the dry season, for the residents do really depend on this team,” explains Ely as she wipes sweat from her brow.

In situations such as this extreme dry season, patrols become essential. “We descend to carry out the monitoring from the morning since the wind becomes strong after 10 a.m.,” Ely states. “Should there be any remaining fire, this wind direction would present a major risk of causing latest fires.”.

Industry observers note that ely, who teaches at a junior high school in the morning, has been involved in the community since it was set up in 2022. The initiative was rooted in Dr. Karmele’s idea of empowering women farmers’ groups so they could receive education and thus abandon the traditional practice of clearing land through slash-and-burn. “I joined so that I might have a platform through which to express my love for environmental conservation and could take direct action in the field,” she notes.

In November 2023, their heroic efforts were officially acknowledged when The Power of Mama was awarded the Indonesian Clean Air Championship Award. But for these women, the real reward is the legacy they leave behind.

Industry observers note that irma remarks that The Power of Mama has taught her a great deal beyond just putting out fires. She has acquired extensive knowledge about the environment, fire prevention, and the protection of river and forest ecosystems; she has a son and is now teaching him to look after nature.

According to recent reports, for Sanchez and the founders, the transformation runs even deeper than the soil they protect. “This isn’t just about putting out fires,” Sanchez says. “It’s about seeing these women become more confident, and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

It has been revealed that the whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking latest ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it indicates in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

One frame shows the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

Industry observers note that the system proves itself where the organization actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, indicates: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, says the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

According to recent reports, charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he notes. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

Recent findings suggest that the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report states.

Recent findings suggest that UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, states: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

The Impossible Comeback: Modern Polaroid 600 Film Is Better Than You Think

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we thought we had seen the last of the Type 600 film back in 2008 when Polaroid revealed it was discontinuing the film.
  • According to recent reports, let’s begin by clearing up a bit of confusion.
  • According to recent reports, the story behind The Impossible Project is pretty remarkable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we thought we had seen the last of the Type 600 film back in 2008 when Polaroid revealed it was discontinuing the film. But then a upcoming organization, composed of folk committed to resurrecting this film format, was formed, calling themselves The Impossible Project. Fast forward almost two decades to today, and all those Polaroid 600 and SX-70 cameras can continue to be supplied with film and make the magic they were originally designed to create. It is an amazing thing, and that is why we are giving Polaroid 600 the Film Friday treatment; it truly is magical stuff.

According to recent reports, let’s begin by clearing up a bit of confusion. The company now known as Polaroid is not the original Polaroid company. What happened is that The Impossible Project acquired the rights to use the Polaroid name in 2017 and rebranded themselves Polaroid Originals. A year or so after that, they dropped “Originals” and rebranded back to the original, and recognizable, Polaroid name. In short: The Impossible Project became Polaroid Originals, which became Polaroid.

According to recent reports, the story behind The Impossible Project is pretty remarkable. When Polaroid announced they were closing up shop in terms of film production, a trio of individuals, Florian Kaps, Marwan Saba, and André Bosman, formed The Impossible Project, which leased one of the old Polaroid plant buildings in the Netherlands and bought a bunch of the old equipment. They then hired ex-Polaroid engineers to help them build a replacement film for the discontinued Polaroid films. They focused on the integral films such as 600, SX-70, and Spectra. Sadly, they were not able to bring back any of the pack films that Polaroid had made.

That early film was pretty awful stuff, but they were attempting to recreate a complex chemical process that Polaroid themselves had spent decades perfecting. Nonetheless, when those first Impossible films hit the market, they quickly proved to be very ephemeral (fading out quickly), extremely finicky (you had to shield the film when it ejected or it would wash out), and highly inconsistent.

But it was a start, and to Impossible’s credit, they continuously revamped the film technology, rolling out multiple successive generations of film. More than a bit unfairly, though, those early generations of the film earned Impossible a negative reputation with many that took years to shake and still persists today. Photographers often talk about complications that Impossible films generated in past iterations but have since been fixed as if they are still happening. What we are getting at, and one of the first things worth discussing with this film, is that the current product far exceeds the often low expectations placed upon it.

Here’s how we describe the current Polaroid film in general. It is not the original Polaroid film, nor is it a resurrected version of it. It is best thought of as its own thing. It definitely has a vintage analog look to it. Whereas Fuji Instax is known for crisp, bright, sharp colors, Polaroid film is a fair bit different.

Let’s start with the Polaroid 600 B&W film. The current generation of this film has a nice amount of contrast to it as well. Shadows can be very crisp and deep, but the highlights are not as clean as those found on Instax. Polaroid 600 B&W has become fairly neutral in its monochrome rendition but still has a touch of an ivory warmth to it. Naturally, as an ISO 640 film, there is a decent amount of visible grain to these images. We feel like the grain of the B&W emulsion is more noticeable than that of the Color emulsion, but, having said that, it is a nice-looking film grain. The developing time for the 600 B&W is stated as 5-10 minutes, with ambient air temperature being one of the biggest factors in an increase or decrease over this time.

The Polaroid 600 Color film, meanwhile, has pretty rich colors but can unpredictably throw in some color casts here and there. The contrast of the Color 600 feels higher than that of the B&W 600. The shadows in Color 600 are deeper and more blocked up. Highlights tend to have a warmer, creamy cast to them as opposed to being a stark white. There is an element of serendipity to the film as well. It is nowhere near as inconsistent as it used to be, but your results will vary from shot to shot. This is part of its charm, in our opinion. Even if the film were perfect, you’d still be running it through old Polaroid cameras that were scavenged at Goodwill or the thrift store. Embrace the element of chance that often arises when using such analog technology. The Color 600 emulsion has a longer developing time than that of the B&W, with a stated range of 10-15 minutes (influenced by ambient temperatures).

Sources indicate that of course, the film’s biggest selling point is its instant nature. There are not many places you can go in the analog world of photography and enjoy seeing your images instantly. For decades, the ability to snap a photo and watch it develop in front of your eyes has charmed people worldwide. It allows you to make a portrait of that interesting passerby and let them walk off with a developed result. Or to get a shot of that special someone and memorialize it in the iconic Polaroid frame. And don’t overlook the fact that each shot is a one-of-a-kind creation. There is no reprinting of the negative; you’ve made a limited-edition series of one. There is a quote by Polaroid’s inventor, Edwin Land, that sums this up beautifully: “[A Polaroid camera] places before you a thing that is more of the thing than the thing was.”.

It has been revealed that before closing, we do have some general tips when shooting with Polaroid 600. The first is to remember that it is an ISO 640 film (as opposed to SX-70, which is ISO 160). This makes Polaroid 600 the better choice for instant photography in slightly dimmer conditions. Most Polaroid 600 cameras have built-in flashes, but not all of them do, so the extra film speed may help. Also, since it is a faster ISO, be more careful when flying with it. Polaroid recommends avoiding airport X-rays at all costs. If you are traveling with Polaroid 600 film, it is best to avoid packing it in your checked luggage (which goes through more powerful X-rays) and to request a hand check at security.

Recent findings suggest that there is also the matter of shielding the film right after it has ejected from the camera. Polaroid film maintains some sensitivity to exposure after it has ejected. The best practice is to immediately tuck it away out of light for the required developing time. It is fine to peek at it now and again, but leaving a developing Polaroid exposed to bright light will result in a faded, washed-out result.

In a recent development, the final point to make in regard to Polaroid film is that it uses the array of cameras made by Polaroid over the several decades that the manufacturer was fully invested in the development of this film. There are dozens of different cameras, oodles of accessories, and all sorts of other fun paraphernalia from the 1970s, ’80s, ’90s, and ’00s to dig up and pair with a box of the modern Polaroid films. One of our staff has a tri-image filter for his Polaroid 600. It’s goofy and definitely very ’80s, but he has a ton of fun with it. So, if you are going to shoot Polaroid, make sure to do some research into the history of the cameras and products made for this film and see what toys you can find to experiment and have fun with! There have also been various Polaroid 600 editions with creative borders, such as the Round Frame. This fun edition operates like normal, but the resulting image is encapsulated in a circular frame instead of a square. Over the years, Polaroid has produced 600 film with various colored borders too.

It has been revealed that lastly, while our entire write-up has been focused on Polaroid 600 film, we can’t sign off without mentioning Polaroid’s i-Type film. Polaroid i-Type film has the same chemistry formulation as Polaroid 600 film, which means it is also a 640 ISO film. The main difference is that Polaroid 600 film includes a built-in battery within the pack. Most vintage Polaroid cameras had no battery of their own, using the battery in the film pack to power the camera and thus ensuring a fresh battery every time you loaded film. Polaroid has now issued modern takes on those vintage OneStep cameras as well as their completely new I-Series. These modern Polaroid cameras have internal rechargeable batteries. So, Polaroid released a less expensive, battery-less version of 600 film called i-Type specifically for these new-generation cameras.

Industry observers note that that is what we have for you today. We’re bringing you both films today at a discounted rate, so head over to our website to shop for both Polaroid 600 and i-Type film, both Color and B&W. While supplies last, of course!

#80240. It Should Have Been Zuiko

It Should Have Been Zuiko

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I remember exactly where I was when I heard what the latest name for the camera brand spun off from Olympus was going to be.
  • According to recent reports, it wasn’t possible to keep Olympus, since the parent organization this fresh company would be spun off from would be retaining and using that brand name.
  • In a recent development, OM System feels like a name decided around a corporate roundtable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I remember exactly where I was when I heard what the latest name for the camera brand spun off from Olympus was going to be. I remember sitting at my desk at my old house, looking at the press release, dumbfounded. There was no way they actually picked that, right?

According to recent reports, it wasn’t possible to keep Olympus, since the parent organization this fresh company would be spun off from would be retaining and using that brand name. Something else needed to be chosen.

In a recent development, OM System feels like a name decided around a corporate roundtable. OM makes a ton of sense as it had been a part of the Olympus brand history for years, so I can see how the suits decided it would be great to keep it as part of the newly introduced firm’s name. OM actually comes from Olympus Maitani, in honor of Yoshihisa Maitani who was a very key camera designer at the company. So by choosing OM, they would intrinsically keep part of the Olympus name, albeit mostly hidden since the average person doesn’t know this history.

And it’s not just one product, it’s a system of cameras and lenses! OM System, on paper, makes logical, rational sense. I don’t have any matter with OM Digital Solutions as the corporate name, but OM System for a product? That’s where you lose me.

In a recent development, it’s uninteresting and, frankly, comes with some serious downsides. What makes it worse is that there is a spectacular brand name that they could have chosen (and still can) that they own as part of the spinoff: Zuiko.

It has been revealed that before becoming Olympus Corporation, the organization was known as Takachiho Seisakusho, named after Mount Takachiho, the peak where mythology states the Japanese gods descended to Earth. When the company expanded from microscopes into Western export markets in 1921, it adopted the trademark Olympus as a Greek mythological parallel to Mount Takachiho.

Takachiho Seisakusho developed its first photographic lens at the Mizuho Optical Research Laboratory in 1936. They needed a name for the new optic, so they combined two kanji characters from the facility’s name: 瑞 (Zui) from Mizuho and 光 (Ko) from Kogaku. The word that was formed from there was Zuiko, which most directly translates to “auspicious light” or “holy light.”.

More loosely translated, it can mean “light of the gods.”.

When Olympus shifted to mirrorless cameras with Micro Four Thirds, it added an “M” to the front of Zuiko to distinguish it from its Four Thirds DSLR lenses. It still uses M.Zuiko today. OM Digital Solutions acquired the Zuiko name entirely as part of its exit from Olympus and still owns it.

It has been revealed that nikon. Canon. Sony (Alpha). Lumix. Sigma. Pentax. Ricoh. Zuiko.

According to recent reports, japanese camera brand names are short, two-syllable words that are easy to fit on the front of cameras and steeped in rich meaning. Sony itself is already two syllables, but Alpha was inherited from Minolta which picked the name because it symbolized peak performance and the beginning of a latest era. Canon is adapted from the Buddhist bodhisattva of mercy, Kwanon. Nikon is a contraction of Nippon Kogaku, the original name of the company. Lumix is a shortened version of luminance, or light.

Sigma comes from the mathematical symbol that means “the sum of parts.” It also was very crucial to Michihiro Yamaki (father of Sigma’s current president Kazuto Yamaki) that a short, two syllable word be the name, as that simplicity would mirror the contemporaries like Canon, Nikon, and Pentax.

Industry observers note that speaking of Pentax, that is a combination of the DSLR pentaprism and the Contax name. Ricoh is very similar to Nikon in that it is a contraction of Riken Kogaku, the pre-war name of the company.

All of these names are strong, quick, and easy to say. They all follow this formula because it a strong foundation and a proven success. Zuiko was right there, bringing with it the entire history of the brand’s power in imaging along with one of the most badass translations among any camera brand. Light of the Gods? My goodness, that’s strong. Fierce, even!

OM System not only has too many syllables, it’s physically too long. The tops of OM System cameras look downright crowded trying to fit those words on there. Embracing Zuiko across its cameras and lenses (and they can drop the M now that the company only makes one type of optic) would have felt like a powerful, intelligent coalescence of the brand’s move into the future by embracing its rich past.

Recent findings suggest that it gets worse when you have OM as part of the company name and the camera names. OM System OM-1 sounds redundant. There is a better way.

It has been revealed that there is no reason OM Digital Solutions has to keep OM System. They can rebrand anytime they like. I argue they should. I know that might sound crazy considering how recently OM System was chosen, but continuing to use it would only be falling into the sunk cost fallacy (the mistake of continuing to invest time, money, and effort into something just because you already spent time on it, even when abandoning it would clearly be the better option).

OM Digital Solutions just threw off the shackles of private equity a few months ago. They are charting a newly introduced path now. There is no better time to put a stamp on that decision and fly a new flag: Zuiko.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

According to recent reports, milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its new identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

The type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

Sources indicate that the system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

Color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the Spotify Discover Weekly cover, with Discover Weekly in white on black over a red to pink gradient, and it runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, indicates the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, photographer and creator Mr. 50mm built a DIY digital rangefinder camera using parts he salvaged from a FED 5 Soviet-era rangefinder and a Panasonic GF3 Micro Four Thirds camera. Mr. 50mm is back with an even better DIY digital rangefinder, and this time it’s APS-C.

According to recent reports, unlike the Micro Four Thirds-based camera Mr. 50mm dubbed the “RGM-79” earlier this year, the new “C7M” uses a larger APS-C image sensor. Mr. 50mm is using the imaging pipeline from the original Canon EOS M mirrorless camera, which Canon unveiled way back in 2012.

Sources indicate that the Canon EOS M features an 18-megapixel APS-C CMOS image sensor, up from the 12.1-megapixel Micro Four Thirds sensor Mr. 50mm salvaged from a Panasonic GF3.

A DIY digital rangefinder requires two donors, though. Rather than the FED 5 rangefinder Mr. 50mm used before, he’s sticking with two Canon cameras this time around. The donor rangefinder is the Canon 7, a rangefinder series that started in 1961 with the original Canon 7 and ended in 1967 with the Canon 7sZ.

Recent findings suggest that although Mr. 50mm hasn’t finalized everything or released a build video yet — it’s in the works — the C7M sure does look impressive thus far. Mr. 50mm is especially impressed with the Canon 7’s finder, which he describes as a “marked upgrade compared to a Fed camera.”.

“The bar wasn’t that high, but the Canon 7 does a lot of things very, very well. You get a brighter finder, you get projected and selectable frame lines, and they’re parallax-corrected,” the builder explains.

Recent findings suggest that further, the Canon 7 uses a Leica M39 screw mount, which is great news for Mr. 50mm. It’s a widely used mount with a ton of lens options on the market.

It has been revealed that while the Canon 7 doesn’t have many controls, that isn’t a downside for Mr. 50mm.

“It doesn’t have that many dedicated controls, which helps reduce the amount of controls I need to either port or figure out if I’m okay to live without. In the end, the digital camera really just has to be able to do two things. It has to accommodate the rangefinder that I’m gonna put on top, and it has to be able to accommodate the mount that I’m using,” he explains.

There are plenty of challenges, though.

In a recent development, “Unfortunately, it isn’t just as easy as disassembling an EOS M and then jamming on latest parts,” Mr. 50mm explains. “There [were] quite a few modifications that needed to be done to the camera to make this work, which I’ll discuss probably in depth in another video.”.

Ultimately, as the video above highlights, he solved the biggest challenges. He says the C7M is “mostly done” and, impressively, it only took a couple of weeks to build from start to finish. Despite a damaging drop during the build, it came together pretty well.

There’s always a catch, though. There are some rangefinder calibration challenges left to figure out, and not everything aligns perfectly yet. Mr. 50mm says he needs to trim back some more material from the EOS M’s parts, although he isn’t sure how much they have left to give.

“Eventually, once things get a bit more ironed out, I’ll draft up a tutorial on how you can actually make your own,” the photographer indicates.

So while the C7M isn’t totally finished yet, it looks very cool and even more promising. Digital rangefinder cameras are expensive, but building one using donor parts and 3D-printed components makes the format significantly more accessible, assuming someone is comfortable with the build process itself.

Sources indicate that although there isn’t a build tutorial yet, it’s still worth considering the potential cost to build a C7M. The Canon EOS M body is around $260 used, not much more than a Canon 7 rangefinder body. If someone has access to a 3D printer, printing the other parts won’t cost much. That’s much less than a brand-new Leica digital rangefinder, for sure.

Canon EOS MBuy used on KEH.comCanon 7Buy used on KEH.com.

Keep an eye on Mr. 50mm’s (excellent) YouTube channel to stay up to date with the project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

Compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

According to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

Heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor plans, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

#80233. Breaking: Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director

Breaking: Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has declared that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has declared that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

This success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he claims. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental indicates of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.

From the Finns, he will also bring an vital lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he notes: “Less talking, more doing.”.

That choice hits before the spine even opens. Sources indicate that inside, the book design drops white margins completely. Full-bleed photographs push straight to the trim edges, anchored only by tiny centered folios along the bottom border so nothing interrupts the torn paper layers. Thereâs no border competing for attention, so cross-gutter pairings drive the pace. On pages 74 and 75, two ripped portraits lock eyes across the fold â a face peeking through jagged olive-green stenciled stock opposite a monochrome eye buried under white shreds and a red slash. Turn to page 259 and red lips above torn yellow ribbons face giant blue halftone teeth bordered by an exposed CMYK color bar. Elsewhere, pages 312 and 313 pair a shredded magenta portrait and clipped white serif type against a violet sheet torn across the middle to reveal a mouth and ghosted lettering.

Sources indicate that edwards told Itâs Nice That the archive grew after lockdowns as a community began trading found dÃ©collages from Manhattan building hoardings, Parisian metro walls, and London Underground theatre posters. Interviews and essays by Sarah Boris, Nick Deakin, Braulio Amado, and experimental drummers Hisham Akira Bharoocha and Jeremy Gustin sit alongside the plates, linking ripped street bills to rhythm and print culture. On pages 354 and 355, a shredded gig poster dated 09.11.24 faces bold white ON A MISSION FOREVER lettering ripping open over yellow underlayers. I Couldn’t Imagine Working With a Photo Editor on a Different Continent

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.
  • In a recent development, I was young and in need of guidance.
  • I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.

In a recent development, I was young and in need of guidance. I found that in the form of my photo editor, whom I’m going to call Gary.

I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.

After I wired him the photos, he would let me know whether I had done a good job or a terrible one.

He would often edit my photos, reframe them slightly, change the crop, cull some of them, or call me up and ask if I had a different angle.

In a recent development, but Gary did far more than that. He was a leader in the newsroom, worked closely with the news editor to shape stories and come up with ideas, and was an excellent salesman.

His vivacious personality helped. He invented nicknames for me and the other photographers, made silly jokes, and was just generally good for staff morale. Not everyone liked the owners, but everyone liked Gary.

According to recent reports, after I had worked there for a few years, the agency was bought out, and Gary moved to a new hub hundreds of miles away. Our relationship was never the same. The new regime was different, and I left soon after.

I thought of Gary this week when the Associated Press officially cut all eight of the remaining photo editor positions in the U.S.

Sources indicate that AP has moved the positions to its hub in Noida, India. The agency notes it has plans to grow the Indian operation to 100 staff members, including video producers.

AP photo editors are legendary: Consider the famous Napalm Girl photograph, for example, when Horst Faas and Hal Buell overruled Carl Robinson’s decision not to wire Nick Ut’s photograph.

Photo editors have played a crucial role in the fortunes of photographers for a very long time, advocating for us while seeing the bigger picture.

According to recent reports, it’s not a question of whether talented photo editors exist in India. Of course, they do. But there’s something valuable about having an editor who understands the local news environment, knows the photographers personally, and can build relationships over years of working together.

Industry observers note that and look, I get it: the press industry is tough. Agency bosses were once raking in vast sums of money — these days they face lousy picture rates from a fractured industry.

Photo editors do not attend a news story in person the way photographers do; therefore, they could theoretically be anywhere. This is a globalized, technologized world: workers in developing countries are technically in competition with workers from the U.S.

But while these significant decisions make sense from a financial point of view, what are the long-term consequences?

Photographers, like my younger self, have fewer opportunities to benefit from a leading light like Gary.

Nowadays, photographers are increasingly expected to be fully formed; the bosses need someone they can rely on to do a good job no matter what. And while there are plenty of great photographers out there who can do that, they all had to cut their teeth somewhere.

As with many other things in life, it feels like the ladder for the younger generation is being removed.

Giga Unveils the AD Italia redesign
